source.title: What Was Once Learned May Need to Be Unlearned: Machine Unlearning for Deprecated API Knowledge in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jin Liu; Yan-Zhong He; Guan-Cheng Lin; Xiao Liu; J. Keung; Xiao Yu; Xiao-Xue Ma

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies several unlearning methods and measures whether deprecated-API behavior is suppressed and general code-generation ability is preserved, but it does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning results on deprecated-API generation, HumanEval capability, and internal-change analyses. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks. The reported PCA and CKA values are described qualitatively in the text rather than given numerically; method hyperparameter choices and cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies eight existing unlearning methods to a new setting: deprecated-API knowledge in three code LLMs. It reports both target suppression (AEM-D) and general-ability preservation (HumanEval), which bears on the first two parts of version A. It runs no recovery attack (fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, prompting), so B–F and A's 'attacks don't recover' part are untested. T3 fits better than T2 because the setting, not the method, is what's new.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that unlearning difficulty varies by library (SciPy hardest, TensorFlow easiest). They further find that APIs deprecated after a model's training cutoff are substantially harder to forget. They frame deprecated-API unlearning as selective knowledge adaptation that should preserve the surrounding completion space.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates API-specific unlearning on behavior-verified code-completion instances using LoRA; it does not reproduce the recovery-attack procedures in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by unlearning method, model, software library, and whether API deprecation occurred before or after the model's training-data cutoff.

fits_no_version.finding: GD gives the best trade-off among methods: strong suppression with preserved specificity, OAMR and HumanEval, and controlled internal changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For deprecated-API unlearning in small code LLMs, GD offers the most favourable forgetting–preservation trade-off; recoverability is not assessed.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggressive methods (RLFT, and in the text GA and SimNPO) suppress the target but disrupt up-to-date-API generation, other-API behaviour and general capability, with broader internal perturbation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggressive unlearning suppresses target behaviour by broadly damaging generation; reversibility is not measured.

record.problems: Only three code models and a Python API-completion benchmark are studied. The results do not include chance-level or never-exposed comparisons, and none of the recovery attacks in the claim are tested. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 3–8 report many additional methods, metrics, libraries, and evaluation splits. The selected rows retain the GD and RLFT Forget Data AEM-D results and HumanEval comparisons across all three models as representative evidence for version A; other method/model/metric combinations and library-specific results are omitted. The paper's qualitative internal analyses are represented by r13–r14; figure-level numerical values are not transcribed.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover suppressed deprecated-API generation; no comparison against a never-exposed model.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation, and no analysis distinguishing blocked access from deletion.
No adversarial rephrasing, jailbreak, language or in-context attack. Held-out Generalization contexts are natural, not adversarial.
No method is evaluated against recovery attacks.

missing.what: GD and other methods on held-out Generalization contexts (e.g., GD AEM-D 5.06/3.77/2.30). Suppression transfers to unseen natural contexts; this bears on A's robustness but is not an attack.
Post-cutoff versus pre-cutoff GD AEM-D (16.01 vs 3.47 on StarCoder2; 12.22 vs 1.67 on DeepSeek-Coder).
Library-specific residual AEM-D; SciPy is much harder (GD 21.16/13.97/16.19 on Generalization data).
DPO, NPO, KL and PROD forgetting rows. AEM-D stays around 9–15 while HumanEval is largely preserved: weaker suppression on the preservation-oriented side of the trade-off.
GA and SimNPO rows: strong suppression with HumanEval drops on some models (e.g., Qwen GA 42.68, SimNPO 41.46).

record.verdict_notes: This study does not address whether unlearning is shallow: no recovery attack is run, so its support for A covers only suppression plus preservation. The 'unlearning' target is a generation tendency observed in at least one of five samples, not factual-knowledge accuracy, so 'chance' means near-zero deprecated-API generation. AdaLoRA-L is a model-editing baseline, not unlearning, and should not be linked to any version.

versions.untested_parts: It does not compare targeted accuracy with chance or with a model that never learned the target, and it does not test whether simple attacks recover the knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery attack is tested.
No activation direction is ablated, and the internal analyses do not test whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No quantization recovery attack is tested.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No method is evaluated against the recovery attacks named in the claim.

relation.reason: Its suppression (AEM-D) and general-ability (HumanEval) results bear directly on the first two parts of version A. The attack-recovery part is untested.

tranche.reason: It applies eight existing unlearning methods to a new setting (deprecated-API knowledge in three code LLMs). It reports suppression and capability results that bear on version A. It proposes no new method for the question, so T3 rather than T2.

statements.correction: For this study: GD on Qwen2.5-Coder-3B cut deprecated-API AEM-D from 33.53 to 5.42 (Table 3), and HumanEval Pass@1 went from 51.83 to 51.22 (Table 5). The targets are deprecated APIs in code completion, not PII. The models are 1.3–3B (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B). No attack was run. Preprint, code available.
statements.problem: The statement cites r1 from this study but says nothing about it. The GA+GD code-LLM privacy-leak numbers (CodeLlama) belong to another study (LLMs4Code). Its conditions ('Models are 7–70B') leave out this study's 1.3–3B models, and its 'why' does not list this study.

statements.correction: RLFT AEM-D (Forget data, %): 0.03, 0.25 and 0.38. HumanEval Pass@1: 51.83→0.61, 31.71→3.66 and 57.32→14.63 (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, StarCoder2-3B, DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B). For A this is limits_scope (l1), not challenges. In the same study GD gets AEM-D 5.42/3.84/2.03 with HumanEval 51.22/31.10/57.93 (supports A, l0).
statements.problem: The numbers are right. But the study is filed under a 'challenges' label, while the record labels this RLFT result limits_scope: by verdict_rules, a cost to general ability is limits_scope. The statement also leaves out that in the same study GD reaches similar suppression with no HumanEval loss.
